problem_statement: The paper frames several core portfolio construction tasks as convex cone programs, including mean–variance optimization, Sharpe-ratio maximization, CVaR minimization, and robust portfolio optimization. It also notes that practical workflows often include additional convex constraints and, in some cases, discrete constraints such as cardinality.
problem_statement_quotes: Many portfolio construction tasks in quantitative finance can be formulated as convex cone programs, notably linear programs (LP), second-order cone programs (SOCP), and semidefinite programs (SDP).

Portfolio optimization is often taught through the Markowitz mean–variance model [Markowitz, 1952], but modern workflows routinely incorporate (a) additional convex constraints (bounds, leverage, sector exposure, turnover), (b) alternative convex risk measures (notably CVaR) [Rockafellar and Uryasev, 2000, 2002], and (c) robustness to estimation error [Ben-Tal et al., 2009, T¨ut¨unc¨u and Koenig, 2004].

This paper presents a self-contained mathematical bridge from: (i) cone programming formulations of core portfolio problems (mean–variance, risk budgeting, CVaR, robust and quasi-convex Sharpe-ratio constructions), to (ii) MW-style feasibility solvers on symmetric cones with explicit Jordan-algebraic structure, to (iii) the SOCP-specific “arrowhead” matrix representation of Lorentz cones and its implications for Gibbs-state preparation, and finally to (iv) a rigorous application-focused analysis of what these ideas do and do not imply for practical finance workloads (conditioning, data access, and discrete constraints such as cardinality).
classical_baseline: The paper treats classical portfolio optimization as being solved with standard convex optimization formulations and compares MW-based approaches against classical interior-point methods. For the LP case it also points to the usual classical multiplicative-weights style algorithms, and for cardinality-constrained portfolios it cites mixed-integer solvers as the practical baseline.

classical_difficulty: The paper says the main classical difficulty is that naive SDP embeddings of SOCP lose structure and can raise per-iteration cost, while practical finance workloads are also affected by conditioning, data access, and discrete constraints. It also states that cardinality-constrained sparse mean–variance optimization is NP-hard, and that poor scaling can make the MW width parameter large and slow convergence.
classical_difficulty_quotes: The same story extends to SOCP because SOCP is a special case of SDP, but a naive reduction can lose structure.

business_stakes: The paper says the relevant real-world stakes are practical finance workloads, including conditioning, data access, and discrete constraints, and it notes that data preparation and constraint engineering are often the bottlenecks rather than the optimization core. It also frames portfolio optimization as a practical finance workflow where robustness to estimation error and realistic constraints matter.
